302.title: Nuns in the Theravada
302.hook: the nuns' order died out in Theravada lands; some now revive it and some do not; both views are held in good faith
302.howItsDone: In Sri Lanka some women are now fully ordained as bhikkhunis, while in Thailand, Myanmar and Sri Lanka many women live as precept-keeping renunciants (mae chi, thilashin, dasa sil mata) in white or pink robes; the main monastic bodies of Thailand and Myanmar do not recognize bhikkhuni ordination.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pabbajja, and your line, for a while: going forth for a season, coming home with honor.

A broom scrapes across a temple courtyard in Thailand, early, before the monks come back from the alms round. The woman holding it has a shaved head and wears white. She keeps eight precepts. She meditates for hours. She may have lived this way for forty years. But she isn't a nun in the full sense the old texts describe, and in Thailand the main monastic body doesn't recognize full ordination for women. Why not? It's a real disagreement, and both sides care about it deeply.
screen: `A WOMAN IN WHITE, SWEEPING AT DAWN.` → `EIGHT PRECEPTS, FORTY YEARS.` → `WHY NOT A FULL NUN?`

segments.voice: The Vinaya tells how Mahapajapati, the aunt who raised the Buddha, asked to go forth. At first he declined. Then, with Ananda speaking for her, the Buddha agreed, and the order of bhikkhunis, fully ordained nuns, began. Their voices survive in the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. For centuries the nuns' order flourished in Sri Lanka, and tradition says Sri Lankan nuns helped give ordination to women in China. Then, in a time of war, the order in Sri Lanka died out, and historians find no clear record of it continuing anywhere else in the Theravada lands. Here is the knot. The Vinaya says a woman's full ordination is given by both nuns and monks together. With no Theravada nuns left, many elders conclude it can no longer be given: the rule needs nuns, and there are none. They are guarding the code exactly as it was handed down. Others point to the nuns of East Asia, whose lineage traces back, in part, to those Sri Lankan women. In recent decades, women have been fully ordained with their help, and communities of bhikkhunis now live in Sri Lanka and in other countries. They are guarding what the Buddha himself began. In Thailand and Myanmar the main monastic bodies don't recognize these ordinations. Meanwhile, many women keep eight or ten precepts in white or pink robes, honored, practicing, teaching. Both views are held in good faith, by people who love the same teaching. The question is still open.
screen: `MAHAPAJAPATI ASKS TO GO FORTH.` · `THE ORDER FADES IN SRI LANKA.` · `THE RULE NEEDS NUNS TO ORDAIN NUNS.` · `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH IN GOOD FAITH.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION IS STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind one woman who practiced: Mahapajapati, who asked first; Kisa Gotami, whom you met with the mustard seed; a grandmother, a teacher, or the woman in white sweeping the courtyard. On each out-breath, if you like, silently wish her well: may she be at ease. Then let her go, and simply sit.
Bhikkhuni. A fully ordained nun: an order that began with the Buddha's aunt Mahapajapati, faded in Sri Lanka, and is being revived by some today.
Your line: the question is still open. Two answers, both given in good faith. Until tomorrow.

303.title: The Path of Purification
303.hook: Buddhaghosa's fifth-century manual: virtue, concentration, wisdom
303.howItsDone: Theravada monks and meditation teachers study the Visuddhimagga as the classic guide to the path, and many meditation centers organize their teaching around its three trainings of virtue, concentration and wisdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhikkhuni, and your line, the question is still open: two answers, both in good faith.

A job interview where they hand you two lines of poetry and say: show us what you understand. That's the story told about a scholar named Buddhaghosa. Sometime in the fifth century he came from India to Sri Lanka, to the Great Monastery at Anuradhapura, hoping to work on the old commentaries kept there. The elders weren't going to hand their library to a stranger. So they gave him a verse and waited. He went away and came back with a book.
screen: `TWO LINES AND A TEST.` → `THE GREAT MONASTERY, SRI LANKA.` → `HE CAME BACK WITH A BOOK.`

segments.voice: The verse comes from a short sutta. A deity asks the Buddha: there's a tangle inside and a tangle outside, and people are caught in it; who can untangle this tangle? The Buddha answers, in paraphrase: a wise person, grounded in virtue, who develops the mind and understanding, ardent and discerning, can untangle it. Buddhaghosa built his whole book on that answer. In Pali it's the Visuddhimagga: visuddhi, purification, and magga, path. Its three parts are the three trainings you can already name. First, sila, virtue: the precepts, the monk's rules, guarding the senses, living simply. Virtue steadies the ground. Second, samadhi, concentration, or calm: forty subjects for meditation, from the breath to the immeasurables to a simple colored disc, matched to a person's temperament, so a restless mind and a heavy mind get different medicine. Calm clears the water. Third, panna, wisdom: seeing the heaps, the chain of causes, and the stages of insight you met in noting, until change, unease and not-self are seen directly. Wisdom sees what the clear water shows. The Sri Lankan chronicle adds a story people still tell: the gods hid the finished manuscript twice, Buddhaghosa wrote it out three times, and when the elders laid the three copies side by side, they matched word for word. Whatever you make of that, the elders gave him the library. For fifteen centuries this book has been the Theravada teacher's map, and the modern Burmese insight methods still lean on it. Three trainings, in order: virtue, calm, wisdom.
screen: `THE TANGLE INSIDE AND OUTSIDE.` · `SILA — VIRTUE STEADIES.` · `SAMADHI — CALM CLEARS.` · `PANNA — WISDOM SEES.` · then, large: `VIRTUE, CALM, WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Walk the three trainings once. Virtue: recall one precept you kept today, even a kind word where a sharp one was ready; calm: let the breath lengthen and the mind settle on it, like silt sinking in a glass; wisdom: notice one thing changing right now, a sound, a sensation, a thought. Name them softly as you go: virtue, calm, wisdom.
Visuddhimagga. The Path of Purification, Buddhaghosa's fifth-century map of the whole path in three trainings.
Your line: virtue, calm, wisdom. A better action, a quieter mind, a clearer look. That's day three hundred three.

what it means: a map of the whole path in three trainings: virtue, calm and wisdom.

what a scholar hears: Buddhaghosa worked from the Sinhala commentaries of the Mahavihara, and the book's forty meditation subjects and stages of insight shaped Theravada teaching for fifteen centuries.

304.title: A Theravada day
304.hook: chanting, the alms round, sitting, walking, sharing merit
304.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries the day usually runs from pre-dawn chanting to the alms round, a meal before noon, sitting and walking meditation, chores and evening chanting; lay people offer food and often pour water while the monks chant, sharing the merit with the dead and all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Visuddhimagga, and your line, virtue, calm, wisdom. Today, the last day with the elders.

A wooden bell, struck slowly, then faster, in the dark. A forest monastery in northeast Thailand, hours before sunrise. Somewhere a gecko answers. Monks come down the paths from their huts with flashlights, and the hall fills with Pali chanting. By the time the sky turns gray, they're walking barefoot into the village with their bowls. For two weeks this path has looked at the way of the elders from the outside. Today: one whole day from the inside, and what its shape is for.
screen: `A WOODEN BELL IN THE DARK.` → `PALI CHANTING BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `BAREFOOT AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: The day opens with chanting. Homage first, the line you learned in the practices camp, "Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa": homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened. Then the refuges, and verses on the qualities of the Buddha, the teaching and the community. Then the alms round, the pindapata. The monks walk in a line, eyes down, and people wait by the road with rice. Nobody asks. Nobody haggles. Food goes into the bowl, the giver may bow, and the monk moves on. Back at the monastery comes the meal, taken before noon, and then the long middle of the day: sitting, walking meditation on a cleared lane, sweeping leaves, sewing, study, a talk from the teacher. In the evening, more chanting. Threaded through it all is the sharing of merit. When lay people offer food, the monks chant a blessing, and the givers slowly pour water from a small vessel into a bowl, letting the good of the gift flow out to their dead and to all beings. Why this shape? Each part trains the others. Chanting sets the mind. The alms round keeps monks humble and villagers generous. Sitting and walking turn calm into seeing. Sharing keeps the good from becoming a private bank account. Now look back at two weeks with the elders. The way of the elders. Three baskets. The forest remembers. Rules as a shelter. Two wings. See clearly. Rising, falling. A map, not a scoreboard. Entering the stream. Give and receive. For a while. The question is still open. Virtue, calm, wisdom. And today, the elders' day.
screen: `CHANTING AT DAWN.` · `THE ALMS ROUND.` · `SITTING, WALKING, SWEEPING.` · `SHARING THE MERIT.` · then, large: `THE ELDERS' DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the day in miniature: if you like, bow once toward whatever you use as a shrine, or just toward the room, then take three slow steps, feeling each foot lift and land. Sit, and let the breath be your whole task. At the end, silently let whatever good came from it go out to someone who has died, and then to everyone; on a slower day, these four steps can fill fifteen minutes.
Puñña. Merit: the good that grows from giving, virtue and meditation, shared and never kept as a private trophy.
Your line: the elders' day. Each part trains the others. Tomorrow, the roof of the world.

screen: `DAY 304 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ROOF OF THE WORLD.`

305.title: The roof of the world
305.hook: Buddhism reached Tibet from the seventh century; its path is called the diamond vehicle
305.howItsDone: Vajrayana Buddhism is practiced in Tibet, Bhutan, Mongolia, the Himalayan regions of Nepal and India, and in Tibetan communities worldwide; practitioners combine Mahayana teaching with mantra, visualization and ritual under the guidance of a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday: puñña, and a whole Theravada day, from dawn chanting to sharing merit. Your line: the elders' day. Today, a new two weeks.

Thin air. Hard light. A wind that never quite stops. On the high plateau of Tibet, barley grows, yaks graze, and the winters are long. Up here, over many centuries, a whole civilization organized itself around the Buddha's teaching: monasteries the size of towns, chants that rumble in the chest, colors everywhere. For two weeks this path walked with the elders. Now it climbs. Today: the roof of the world, and the name of its path.
screen: `THIN AIR, HARD LIGHT, WIND.` → `BARLEY, YAKS, LONG WINTERS.` → `A PATH BUILT UP HERE.`

segments.voice: Buddhism reached Tibet in waves. Tibetan tradition says the seventh-century king Songtsen Gampo married princesses from Nepal and China, and each brought an image of the Buddha to Lhasa. Later, King Trisong Detsen invited two teachers from India: the scholar Shantarakshita and the master Padmasambhava, whom Tibetans call Guru Rinpoche, the precious teacher. Stories say Padmasambhava tamed the spirits of the land, and together they founded Samye, which tradition remembers as Tibet's first monastery. More teachers followed over the centuries, carrying texts across the Himalayas to be translated with great care. The path they built is the Vajrayana. Yana means vehicle. Vajra is harder to pin down, and that's the point. In old India it was the thunderbolt of the god Indra. In Buddhism it became the diamond: nothing can break it, and it cuts through everything. Tibetans call it dorje. In ritual, a teacher holds a small metal dorje in the right hand and a bell in the left: method and wisdom, together. The diamond vehicle keeps the Mahayana heart, the wish to wake up for all beings, and adds its own tools: mantras, visualizations, rituals, and a close bond with a teacher. You'll meet each of them over these two weeks. Today it's practiced in Tibet and among Tibetans in exile, in Bhutan, Mongolia, the Himalayan regions of Nepal and India, and beyond. Like the elders' way, it's learned here on its own terms, beside the others, never above or below them. The diamond vehicle.
screen: `KINGS, PRINCESSES, AN IMAGE IN LHASA.` · `GURU RINPOCHE AND SAMYE.` · `VAJRA: THUNDERBOLT, THEN DIAMOND.` · `DORJE AND BELL — METHOD AND WISDOM.` · then, large: `THE DIAMOND VEHICLE.`

segments.voice: Picture the high plateau: thin, cold air on your face, a sky so blue it's almost dark, a white monastery far off on a ridge. Let the breath go slow, the way nobody hurries up a hill at that height, and feel how small and steady it is inside all that space. When the mind wanders, come back to the wide sky.
Vajrayana. The diamond vehicle: the Buddhism of Tibet and the Himalayas, named for what cannot be broken and cuts through.
Your line: the diamond vehicle. Steady as a diamond, sharp enough to cut. Day three hundred five, and the climb begins.

306.title: Om mani padme hum
306.hook: the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara, whom Tibetans call Chenrezig
306.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists recite Om mani padme hum aloud or under their breath through the day, often counting on a string of 108 beads, and carve or paint it on stones placed along paths and on walls that walkers pass on their right-hand side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vajrayana, the Buddhism of Tibet and the Himalayas, named for what cannot be broken and cuts through. Your line: the diamond vehicle.

Stones with letters carved into them line the trails of the Tibetan Himalaya, sometimes painted, sometimes piled into long walls taller than a person. On a bench in Dharamsala or Kathmandu, an old woman murmurs, beads slipping through her fingers, the same short sound again and again. Some people keep count on their beads from morning to night. The stones and the woman are saying the same six syllables.
screen: `CARVED STONES BY THE PATH.` → `BEADS AND A MURMUR.` → `THE SAME SIX SYLLABLES.`

segments.voice: Om mani padme hum. In Tibetan it's usually om mani peme hung. It's the mantra of Avalokiteshvara, whom you met in the Heart Sutra, looking deep. Tibetans call him Chenrezig, the one who looks with eyes of compassion, and Tibetan tradition regards the Dalai Lama as his emanation. The mantra appears in an Indian Mahayana text, the Karandavyuha Sutra, and traveled to Tibet with the teachers. What does it mean? Om is a sacred syllable Buddhism shares with older Indian traditions. Mani means jewel. Padme has to do with the lotus. Hum is a seed syllable with no dictionary meaning. So the familiar English reading is the jewel in the lotus. That phrase became popular through European scholars, and some scholars read the grammar differently, perhaps as a call: O jewel-lotus one. Nobody can settle it for certain. Tibetan teachers tend to explain it by what it does. The jewel is the wish to help others. The lotus, which grows clean out of mud, is wisdom. Together they're the whole path: compassion and wisdom joined. Some teachers also link the six syllables to the six realms of rebirth, each syllable easing the suffering of one. And the stones? Carving the mantra, or paying someone to carve it, is an act of merit, and the stones sit where travelers pass, kept on their right as they walk. The mantra is so short that anyone can carry it. That's much of the point. The jewel in the lotus.
screen: `CHENREZIG — EYES OF COMPASSION.` · `JEWEL, LOTUS, TWO SYLLABLES.` · `THE MEANING IS STILL DEBATED.` · `COMPASSION AND WISDOM JOINED.` · then, large: `THE JEWEL IN THE LOTUS.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, say om mani padme hum softly twenty-one times, counting on your fingers or on beads if you have them, more a murmur than a chant. If saying it doesn't feel right for you, listen to it inwardly, or just count twenty-one breaths. When you finish, let the sound fade and sit in what's left.
Chenrezig. The bodhisattva of compassion, called Avalokiteshvara in Sanskrit, whose six-syllable mantra is om mani padme hum.
Your line: the jewel in the lotus. Kindness and clear seeing, joined. That's day three hundred six.

307.title: Wheels and flags
307.hook: prayer wheels turned by hand, prayer flags in the wind: the mantra carried by movement
307.tomorrow: Four thoughts that turn the mind
307.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists spin hand-held and monastery prayer wheels clockwise, often while walking around a temple, and hang five-colored prayer flags on passes and rooftops, often renewing them at the Tibetan New Year and retiring faded ones respectfully.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chenrezig, the bodhisattva of compassion, and his six syllables, om mani padme hum. Your line: the jewel in the lotus.

A few weeks ago you met a koan: two monks arguing over a flag in the wind. Is the flag moving, or the wind? Today there are thousands of flags, strung across mountain passes, from rooftops, over bridges, snapping in color against the sky. Beside the monastery walls stand rows of painted drums on spindles, and pilgrims walk past, spinning each one with the right hand. Nobody's reading anything. And yet, Tibetans say, the words are being said.
screen: `THE FLAG AND THE WIND, AGAIN.` → `THOUSANDS OF FLAGS ON A PASS.` → `DRUMS SPINNING UNDER HANDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the wheel. Tibetans call it a mani wheel, after yesterday's mantra. Inside the drum is a long, tightly rolled scroll printed with om mani padme hum, over and over. Turn it once, clockwise, and tradition counts it as saying every mantra inside. Some wheels are small, held in the hand, with a weight on a chain to keep them spinning. Some are giant, in their own little houses. Some sit in streams so the water turns them day and night, and some spin in the rising heat of a lamp. Now the flags. A traditional set has five colors in a fixed order: blue, white, red, green, yellow, often linked to sky, wind, fire, water and earth. Each is printed with mantras and prayers, and many carry a horse with a jewel on its back: the lungta, the wind horse. The flags aren't hung to bless the person who hung them. They're hung high so the wind carries the blessing outward, to every being it touches. And they're meant to fade. Sun and wind wear the print away, and in a sense that's the mantra going out into the world. New flags are often hung at the Tibetan New Year, and old ones are retired with respect, never tossed on the ground. Does a spinning drum really count? Tibetans answer in different ways. For some, the turning is enough. Some teachers add that it means most when the mind turns with it, toward others. Either way, the teaching rides on movement: hands, water, fire, air. The wind carries it.

segments.voice: Turn something slowly, a cup in your hands or just your hand drawing a clockwise circle in the air, and with each turn send a small wish outward, to no one in particular: may someone somewhere be at ease. After three or four turns, set it down, rest your hands, and feel the stillness after the movement. Then let the breath do the turning.
Lungta. The wind horse printed on Tibetan prayer flags, carrying blessings outward on the wind to every being they touch.
Your line: the wind carries it. A blessing that's sent, not kept. See you tomorrow.

308.title: Four thoughts that turn the mind
308.hook: precious human life, death, karma, the faults of samsara
308.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often recite and reflect on the four thoughts at the start of each practice session, and they form the first part of the preliminary practices (ngöndro) taught in all the Tibetan schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lungta, the wind horse, and wheels and flags that carry the mantra outward. Your line: the wind carries it. Today, the end of the week.

A doctor's call. A birthday with a zero on the end. A friend who was fine last month, and isn't. Most people change direction only after a jolt like that. For a week or two, everything looks different: what matters, what doesn't, how you want to spend your hours. Then the feeling fades and the old grooves take over. Tibetan teachers noticed this long ago, and built the jolt into the very start of the path, on purpose, so it wouldn't depend on bad news.
screen: `A DOCTOR'S CALL. A BIRTHDAY.` → `EVERYTHING LOOKS DIFFERENT.` → `THEN THE OLD GROOVES RETURN.`

segments.voice: In Tibetan practice, four reflections come before everything else, and people return to them for a lifetime. First, precious human life. Tibetan teachers borrow an image the Buddha gives in the Pali discourses: a blind turtle in the great ocean rises to the surface once every hundred years, and a wooden yoke with one hole drifts on the waves. The turtle will put its head through that hole, the Buddha says, sooner than a being who has fallen into the lower realms will win back a human birth. So this life, with the time and freedom to learn anything at all, is rare. Second, death and impermanence. Death is certain; its time is not. Third, karma: actions have results, and the small ones add up. Fourth, the faults of samsara, the round of birth and death: even the good parts don't last, and chasing them never quite satisfies. The twelfth-century teacher Gampopa taught all four in a famous book, and the preliminary practices set them in this order, which matters. First you see how lucky you are. Then how short the time is. Then how much your actions count. Then that more chasing won't fix it. Together, they swing the mind around, like a boat in the current, toward the path. Now look back at the week. For a while. The question is still open. Virtue, calm, wisdom. The elders' day. Then the climb: the diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it. And today: turn the mind.
screen: `PRECIOUS HUMAN LIFE.` · `DEATH IS CERTAIN, ITS TIME IS NOT.` · `ACTIONS HAVE RESULTS.` · `CHASING NEVER QUITE SATISFIES.` · then, large: `TURN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Choose one of the four and stay with it: for precious human life, picture the turtle and the yoke, then look at your own hands, here, with time to sit; for death, rest in the thought that this breath is one of a limited number. Don't push toward a feeling; let the thought sit beside you the way you'd sit beside a friend. When the mind wanders, return to the one you chose.
Gampopa. The twelfth-century teacher who taught the four thoughts in a famous book: precious human life, death, karma, and the faults of samsara.
Your line: turn the mind. Four thoughts, and the boat swings toward the path. That's the week.

fork.setup: you've just heard that human life is precious and death's timing unknown. a Tibetan teacher asks what you'll do with that. which answer fits the four thoughts?
options: panic and try to do everything at once.
let it turn the mind toward what matters, steadily.
forget it; it's too gloomy.
fork.reveal: the four thoughts aren't meant to frighten but to turn the mind, like a boat in the current, toward the path.

original.note: Tibetan blo ldog rnam bzhi: blo (mind) + ldog (turn back) + rnam bzhi (the four): the four thoughts that turn the mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: gloomy thoughts to make you feel bad.
what it means: four reflections that turn the mind toward the path: luck, urgency, care, and seeing through the chase.

what a scholar hears: Gampopa's Jewel Ornament of Liberation teaches all four early on, after buddha-nature; as the 'common' preliminaries of ngöndro they are shared by Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug alike.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 129, Balapandita Sutta (the blind turtle and the yoke)
Gampopa, Jewel Ornament of Liberation (the four thoughts)
